en: O Laugākṣi, Mahendra, Malaya, Sahya, Śuktimat, Vṛkṣaparvata, Vindhya, and Pāriyātra— these seven are the principal mountain ranges (kulaparvatas). 1.
Due to the distinctions of the Vedas, Vaiṣṇava, Vaidika, Ārhata, Śaiva, and Saura, this is known as the "Sixfold Salutation" by sages proficient in knowledge.
Om! Having paid homage to the Self-Existent One, to Brahmā, whose form is the Veda.
From the Vedas, from the deities, and likewise from the composers of the mantras,
I shall proclaim in due order the entire *ārṣa*, *chandas*, *daivata*, and *viniyoga* according to the Ārāyaṇīyaka tradition.
By this [knowledge] being correctly understood, one attains longevity, purification of fame, sons, and likewise a full residence in heaven;
as well as freedom from disease, the status of a Brāhmaṇa, and the role of a priest for those who employ him in sacrifices.
If one performs or causes a sacrifice to be performed merely as a ritual act,
he becomes worse due to the exhaustion of the Vedic meters; moreover,
upon death, he attains total obscurity and does not enter a womb again.
But he who knows the seers and the meters within each mantra is honored above thousands of divine Manus;
all honor him, as well as one who is worshiped and prosperous.
One who is free from fear may obtain the fear of a deity.
That mantra by which one whose self is purified through practiced austerity perceives [the truth], its seer is said to be that very person; for indeed, Brahmā is the seer of everything. 9–10.
Why is the seer (ṛṣi), who knows all as Brahman, called "the highest" (atyaya)?
Because both the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) and the Supreme Self (paramātman) are to be known; therefore, both of them are indeed [the object of knowledge].
Furthermore, O You, Agni is made new again from what is worn out by means of the Vedic meters (chandas).
The Śruti declared that previously this [portion] was to be cut off by the choice of the Brahman priest;
it is stated as a *saṃyājyā* distinguished by its meter in optional sacrifices (*kāmyeṣṭi*), and the entry of the Hotṛ, who possesses that form, is stated among the duties of the Brahman. 12–13.
Because they have departed from that which is covered by the Chatas and the Bhichas,
and because they have gone away from the sacrifice and all the meters, therefore those [sacrifices] must be known through the Veda.
For one who does not know the meter, the sacrifice, the birthplace, and likewise the accent—
The thunderbolt of speech acts upon them and extends over them like a sharp goad;
I shall now describe the characteristics of those Yajus mantras from the beginning—having known this, the wise man should apply it everywhere. 15–16.
The single-syllable [meter] and so forth, in sequence: Mā, Pramā, and likewise Pratimā; then Astry, Vayakṣarapaṅkti, Gāyatrī, and Uṣṇik;
as well as Anuṣṭubh, Bṛhatī, Paṅkti, Virāṭ, and Triṣṭubh. (17)
Jagatī and Atijagatī, Śakvarī and likewise Atiśakvarī; Aṣṭi and Atyaṣṭi, Dhṛti and likewise Atidhṛti;
Kṛti, Prakṛti, Akṛti, and likewise Vikṛti and Saṃkṛti. (18–19)

*Atikṛti* and *utkṛti* follow in sequence, making thirty-six; that which exceeds these is *aticchandas*, and one should apply it to the *yajus*. (20) I shall describe the meters (*chandāṃsi*) in relation to the *ṛks*; one should fill out a deficient foot with barley-grains (*yava*).
By means of their own four feet, all these [varieties] come into being.
Indeed, in this very same way, whether consisting of one, two, three, or four feet, they are all [classified as] *paṅkti* or *akṣara*; and when there are four feet, it would be *utkṛti*. (21–22)

When lacking the *hmadaika* (the *praśleṣa*) and possessing an excess of *dakṣya* (the *kampa*), there is the *virāṭ*; the *pluta* vowels are always *udātta*. The Brāhmaṇa Vasiṣṭha is *gāyatra* and *anudātta*;
the Kṣatriya Bharadvāja is *traiṣṭubha* and *svarita*; the Vaiśya Gautama is *jāgata* and [has] the *udātta*. 23.

Agni is the deity of the udātta accent, Vāyu of the anudātta, and Sūrya of the svarita; however, there is doubt regarding this because the Śūdras possess speech characterized by flames, sparks, and wind. 24.
Ṣaḍja, vṛṣabha, gāndhāra, as well as ṛṣabha, pañcama, madhyama, and niṣāda are the seven notes (svaras).
Niṣāda and gāndhāra are high [notes], while vṛṣabha and ṛṣabha are low [notes]. 25.
The remaining notes—Ṣaḍja, Madhyama, and Pañcama—are to be known as svarita (circumflex).
One should know that the white [color] is udātta (acute), the red is indeed nīca (grave), and one should recognize the dark [color] as svarita; these are the deities of the non-udātta. 26–27.
For a *svarita* vowel that is low-pitched (*nīca*), the *udātta* accent is prescribed; for one produced in the palate (*tālu*) or the throat (*garbha*), it is likewise *svarita*, as is the *pracaya*.
Furthermore, there is the low-pitched (*nīca*), the entirely unaccented (*sarvānudātta*), and the intermediate tone (*antara*) there.
The *pracaya*, the *tālugarbha*, and likewise the *sannatara*—in the system of Ārāyaṇīya, it should be known that speech touches [the palate] but the hand does not;
furthermore, that [touching] is to be understood as twofold, occurring both before a vowel and before a consonant. 29–30.
For those who contemplate the syllables established by the two colors of the pigeon,
its *mātrā* is said to be in the heart, its *anumātṛkā* in the head, and the *aṇumātrā* of the color in the tip of the nose. 31.

Just as a pearl, overwhelmed by the blue luster of Indra (sapphire), assumes a dark-blue appearance, even so the entire tone, when endowed with the quality of the nasal resonance (*nāsikya*), attains the state of *raṅga*. From the heart arises the *raṅga*, which, like bell-metal, possesses its own distinct sound.
The short vowel has one mātrā, and the long has two; "rachvā" is given as an illustration.
When followed by a voiceless consonant, they call it *raṃga*; that which is produced through the mouth and nose is nasalized (*anunāsikya*); "ṛm̐ bhūḥ" is the illustration. 33–34.

One should know that the letter *ha* joined with the fifth [consonant] of its class, even when combined with a vowel (*uccaiḥ*), is "chest-born" (*urasya*); however, some say it is "throat-born" (*kaṇṭhya*) when it stands alone.
When an *anusvāra* is present in the preceding word and situated before it [the *ha*], [it is also so]. 35.
Then one should know it to be short; "having established" is the illustration. And sometimes, above the *anusvāra*, it is seen as contracted (*saṃvṛtta*);

it should be known as long, for the rule is "one hears the sacrifice as long. It should be known as long; the vision is that one hears the sacrifice as long. [The vowel] with the letter *na* is neither *alona* nor *alamba-oṣṭhī*, nor is it entirely nasalized (*sarvānunāsika*).
One who stammers or has a tongue that falters is unfit to perform the ritual application (prayoga).
But he who studies [the Veda] devoid of its phonemes, lacking the correct formation and accents, is consumed by the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas and goes to a low birth.

A mantra that is employed in sacrifices by a sacrificer while deficient in its proper accent or phonetic form destroys his body, life-span, progeny, and cattle. [39] That which has come from an improper source, that which is consumed [without purity], that which is recited without having bathed, and that which is not firmly established in oneself— [these are likewise destructive].

That which is uttered with a beautiful voice from one's own mouth shines like Brahman. (40) One should know those letters in which *ya*, *la*, *va*, and *d* are seen joined with *śa*, *ṣa*, and *sa* as "hairy" (*lomaśa*); the remaining ones are "hairless" (*alomaśa*). (41)

When the first [nasal] is joined with a following *ūṣman* (sibilant), one should apply the second [nasal] to the preceding consonants; this occurs in two types of cases, as in the word *matsyaḥ* or *tat savituḥ*.
Furthermore, when *ṅ*, *ṇ*, or *ṇ* are at the end of a word, they remain before *ś*, *ṣ*, or *s*.
When are they obstructed? Let this illustration be set aside.

Like the short vowel and so forth, there is that which follows the calf, and that which follows after the calf; the bearer of ripeness shines with splendor, yet the ant is neither short nor long. 43–44.
These four movements should be known by those who contemplate the syllable:
*pipīlikā-prayāma*, *mātrā*, *sthāna*, and *vatsānusāriṇī*.
In *vatsānusṛti*, there is a *dvy-aṇu* [movement] in the *avakavatī*; in *aṇupāda*, there is an *aṇu*; in *sthāna*, there is an *avarca*; and in *dvyaṇu*, there is a *dvyaṇu*.
The measure of a *mātrā* is that of an *anuvāka*; the measure of a *sthānaka* is the time it takes to milk a cow. 46.

Where an *anusvāra* is preceded by [a vowel] and followed by the two [consonants *y* and *v*], one should know that as a case of *parasavarṇa*; therein, one should designate a doubling (*dvitva*). 47.
I shall now explain the four *svarabhaktis* in their proper order:
one should know *hariṇī* for the pair *ra* and *ha*; *charviṇī* for the pair *ra* and *śa*; *utkariṇī* for the pair *la* and *śa*; and *dhātrī* for the pair *ra* and *sa*. (48)
That which occurs between the letters *repha* and *śakāra* in the *haṃsapada* [sandhi] is the *svarabhakti*.
One who employs these *svarabhaktis* should avoid three faults:
namely, being out of tune (*visvara*), being discordant (*virasa*), and likewise the fault of being grasped incorrectly (*grāhyadoṣa*). 49–50.
In sequence, one should perform the contraction at the tip of the thumb (50);

at the end of *sāṃ*, one should form the shape of a fist; at the end of *tyāṃ*, there should be the pressing together of the fingers; and at the end of *yoḥ*, the index finger (*pradeśinī*) should be contracted. (51)
Likewise, at the end of a consonant cluster (gaṇa) or a final consonant, there is the release of the joint;

however, when there is contact between the palms, they know that the extension of the fingers and thumbs occurs at the nails, but not for a sibilant (ūṣman), a semivowel (antaḥstha), or a nasal (na). 52.
Just as the Lord of Nāgas, Saumatta, [divides] foot by foot into three parts,
so too should each word, from beginning to end, be carefully examined; for the application of vowels such as the *anudātta* and others occurs at the beginning of every phoneme.
One should indicate that there is a double acute accent (*udātta*) on both the first and the second [syllables].

If a contact (*sparśana*) is observed at the junction of the release (*mokṣa*) and the grasping (*grahaṇa*), one should perform a modulation (*sāraṇā*) upon that contact; thus, the release occurs previously. 55

[The following are] words with the acute accent on the final syllable (antodātta), those with the acute accent on the first syllable (ādyudātta), those with the acute accent [on the middle], those without the acute accent (anudātta), those with the low tone (nīca), those with the circumflex (svarita), those with the acute accent on the middle syllable (madhyodātta), those with the circumflex [on the middle], those with two acute accents, and not those with three acute accents; these are the word-arrangements (padaśayyā):
*agniḥ*, *somaḥ*, *pra vo vīryam*, *haviṣā svah*, *vanaspatiḥ*. 56.
In the example beginning with "indrābṛhaspatibhyām," the enraged teacher says:
"One should employ short and protracted vowels, and [use] the nasalized vowel at pauses; however, for one's own verses and the like, one should indicate the *natya* (dramatic) and the consonants. 57.
Furthermore, the repeated words in the *Saptacārāyaṇīyaka* were set aside; the sage Śākalya declared that there are two [types of svarita] in the *Dvevāvya*:
where there is a tremor following an *anudātta*, there the *pṛṣṭaga* occurs at a distance of two finger-breadths.
The wise one should cause [the vowel] joined with a short sound to vibrate;
having descended from the udātta accent by exactly one and a half finger-breadths,
he should then produce the vibration, while the hand remains in that very place.
Where there is a tremor following a *svarita* accent, the hand should move upward by one finger-breadth; when it reaches the ear, it should vibrate and extend beyond half a finger-breadth.
However, where there is a single tremor between two [vibrations], it should be thick at that point. 61–62.
The second [type of *pracaya*] is one finger-breadth higher than the first, which is one and a half fingers.

Regarding the planets beginning with Aṃtya (the last), there is an accumulation (*pracaya*) when there is an absence of others; furthermore, in the case of repetition (*punarukta*) and high/low (*uccanīca*), there is an accumulation of the repeated [note] due to its being high, and in the case of the first two [notes], there is an accumulation of the repeated [note] when there is an absence of others. 63–64.
The accumulation of *visandhi* and other such phenomena is not desired as if they were non-existent (65).
For the purpose of introducing the *agniṣṭoma*, the sequences of words for *praṇītā*, *triṣṭubh*, *jagatī*, *anuṣṭubh*, *triṣṭubh*, and so forth, are indeed desired.
For *jyotiṣkṛt*, *svaryat*, and others, the first two [consonants] are the *sajihvāmūlīya* and *upadhmānīya*; in both cases where there is a *repha*, the first two are with the *repha* (66).

The words *ahorātra*, *sadaḥ*, *havirdhāna*, and so forth, when used in the dual number; those ending in *pṛkta* except for *ava*; those that are not neuter except for the fourth case; those beginning with *navadhā* except for the fourth case; *bhṛṇahā* and *avi*; and *hāsaṃskṛtam*—these remain unseparated (i.e., do not undergo sandhi).
He, who was watchful, cast down the Kakubhas, the Mānasas, and the thieves.

Thus, in the *Cārāyaṇīya* [recension], these [sections] remain unbroken; the word "samadveti" is followed by the word "śabda. (68) In the *Bahvṛca* [recension], the final section of the *digvācam* is the unbroken *pada*; from that which follows, the subsequent portion belonging to the right wing [of the *śastra*] is "viṣṇor nu kaṃ vīryāṇi pravocam," while the subsequent portion belonging to the left wing is "bhrātṛvyahvoka."
"Uttārāṇi" (crossings) and so forth are terms that do not denote actual crossings; rather, those southern meters (*chandāṃsi*) which are unbroken are called "uttarāṇi.
Thus, "uttaram" and so forth refers to a broken [meter] and the *niṣasā*, as well as the *niṣasūṣaṇā*. 69.
*Niṣasūṣaṇā*.

The two *dṛṣu* [roots] are followed by *na*, and there is the substitution of *ṇa* for *na* after a preceding word; *svaḥ* and *svarga* denote heaven; *jātya* is for excellence; *sam-ūṣati* is used in that sense; there is no elision (*lopa*) of *t* in that case;
*agniḥ* has the quality of *sva*; *prāhiṃsīt* (he struck); *agniḥ tvām ātrayat* (Agni protected you); *aditiḥ tvā ayastvā asadan* (Aditi placed you in your seat). 70–71.

In such cases as *āyuste viśvato dadhat*, although there is no *ṭ*-sound (*ṭakāra*) even for those [words] beginning with *na vyepaiḥ*, there is a *ṭ*-sound in the word *pṛthivī* when it follows [the aforementioned conditions]. In the *saṃhitā* (continuous text), however, there is no [ṭ-sandhi] in *svarṇadharma-svarṇajyotiḥ*. In the *Cārāyaṇīyaka* [recension], in the passage *idānīm vā vidhavā tvaṣṭa...*, the tenth and eleventh [syllables] of the *indrāṇā* [verse] are short vowels, yet they are joined (*śliṣṭa*) and not separated (*aviṣṭa*). Words such as *piṣṭa*, *ślīṣṭa*, *avedara*, *oṣadhi*, *vana*, *sni*, and *bahumitra* have short vowels; however, words like *bhismakhara* and *khaṇḍita* are exceptions, as in the phrase *svapiṣat tv avarje*, where it is "broken" (*khaṇḍita*). 73.
The word *preṣadhi* is short-voweled when followed by *tam* in a mantra; it is accented on the first syllable in a mantra—this is the recitation of the Śikhya.
(74) The seventh [chapter] begins with *ghaśca*; the deities are Avasvān, Agni, Gāyatrī, Tārā, Keśinī, Dhātṛ, Revatī, Svāhā, Pipīlikā, Tvāṣṭṛ, and Vāyavyā; these are the nine meters. (75)
In their respective forests—the eastern, the middle, and the northern—three tempos each are praised in succession: the fast, the medium, and the slow.
For just as a herd of cows, having left their calves behind during the night, returns to them at dawn.

Even Brahmā proceeds in that same manner; likewise, the messenger Praṇava comes to the mouth of the crooked one (Vakrā). 77. In the mouth of Vāśu, one should utter the speech that follows the tradition (Āmnāya), which is endowed with the power of the Sāman, which is true, swift, and unhindered, and which is to be fashioned [according to the occasion]. 78.
The Sāman is to be understood by the word *sāma*; that breath (*prāṇa*) is eightfold, and I shall declare their characteristics to you:
the *jātya*, the *abhinihita*, the *kṣaipra*, the *praśliṣṭa*, the one known as *tairovyañjana*, and the *tairovirāma*. (79–80)
Likewise, the *tathābhāvī*, the *tathosvāra*, the *pādavṛtta*, and the eighth, the *tathāṣṭama*;
these four should proceed diagonally (*tiryañc*), while the others go in two rows.
Just as when an arrow is released from a bow, the string returns again. 81.

One should return to one's own place when the vowel has reached the hand; likewise, for those possessing qualities, there is the attainment of the three [goals] such as birth and so forth in their entirety.
When the hand returns again, it reaches that high state which is the supreme goal.

One should know that the *svarita* [accent] consists of three finger-breadths (*tryaṅgula*). When it is not situated in a *pracaya* (continuous) [passage], it is one finger-breadth; when followed by a low tone (*nīca*), it is understood as six finger-breadths. In the threefold *svarita*, one should apply the horizontal placement of the word (*tiryakpada*). If the letter *a* is above [the *svarita*], even though it has moved upward, it should be treated as if it had not moved. The *svarita* of the *abhinihita* type is sharp; therefore, it should be somewhat softer than that.
A *praśliṣṭa* [svarabhakti] is somewhat soft and swift; therefore it is so designated. From the *kṣaipra* [svarabhakti], it is softer; from the *jātya*, it becomes even softer.
Because there is an interruption [of the vowel] therein, it is called *tairovyañjana*. 85–86.

Among all the metrical feet (pādavṛtta), that which is distinguished by being made slow is superior; it is a word whose syllable, whether containing the letter *ya* or otherwise, is circumflex (*svarita*).
A vowel preceded by a low tone (*nīca*) or not so preceded is called a homogeneous (*sajātya*) vowel.
The word *ājyam* [is so called] when the vowel *a* is seen between two acute (*udātta*) syllables;

that which is grave (*anudātta*) is called *abhinihita*. That very same [vowel] is called *aja* when it is followed by *u*, provided these two vowels, *ya* and *va*, occur somewhere [in the preceding position]. 88–89.
One should know that the characteristic of the *kṣaipra* [sandhi] occurs invariably when there is a following vowel;
where there is elision of *yat*, it is joined with the vowel *i* itself, as in *udāttaṃ* and *anudāttaṃ*, and the *praśliṣṭa* [sandhi], as in *abhītthatām*.
Whatever word is seen with a circumflex accent (*svarita*) preceded by an acute accent (*udātta*), this is called *tairovyañjana* when it occurs in a passage containing many circumflex accents.
Where there is a circumflex accent immediately following an *avagraha*, [it is likewise so designated]. 91–92.
One should know that [a word] has a *tirovirāma* (internal pause) if there is an *avagraha* in an *udātta* accent;
where there are both high (*ucca*) and low (*nīca*) accents, and where there is also an *avagraha* in the low accent,
one should recognize it as being subject to such treatment— as is illustrated by the example *tanūnaptre*.

Where there is a svarita accent on a vowel and where there is a hiatus in the *saṃhitā*, the wise declare that one should recognize this as *pādavṛtta*. At the end of a quarter-verse (*pāda*), however, there should be a pause; this is remembered as *bahvāloka*.
The name *ardharca-vaiyuta* occurs at the end of a *ṛc*; *bhuga-gama* occurs at the end of a *dūtā* meter; in the *vṛtti* called *trikalā*, it is *madhyamā*; in the *pañcakalā*, it is *vilambitā*.
(96) The essence of the *gāyatrī* is white in form, while the *uṣṇih* has the form of a *sāraṅga*.
The golden form of the quarters is entirely Ānuṣṭubh;
the red form of the Bṛhatīs is likewise Tila, which is Pāṅkta; furthermore, the golden form of the Triṣṭubhs is said to be Gaura, which is Jāgata. 97–98.
From that [the seed] came the Chandas; from them, Śyāvāśva; then again, Nakula among the one-footed ones, and Vabhru among the two-footed;
and the Sāraṅga is said to have a white-and-black form.
The first, the last, and the third [consonants], along with *ya*, *la*, *va*, *śa*, *ṣa*, and *sa*, should be joined with the numbers one through twenty by doubling them;
in the school of Ārāyaṇīya, there is a modification of the vowels and the final letter is *auṃ*.
In all instances, those who follow other treatises desire the forms *sandhimat*, *ichatva*, and *kāretva*;
however, these two [forms] are the original base (*prakṛtibhāva*) of the word *aṅga* in a mantra, but not in a Brāhmaṇa—except for the case of "from limb after limb" (*utsādato aṅgādaṅgāt*). 102.

In the same way, the *ekāra* resulting from the modification of the sound [of the preceding vowel] remains in its original form (*prakṛti*) when followed by another *ekāra*. 103. When followed by other words such as *advān*, *amā*, and so forth, there is preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*).
In the case of *uru-juṣāṇaḥ* and *vṛṣṇaḥ*, there is no vocalic modification (*vivṛtti*) before the word *asi*. 104.
O Bhavati Garbhabhadra—
since they have indeed attained the state of immortality by being concealed within the meters (chandas),
all the meters are therefore to be known through sacrifice. 105
But if one does not know the word, the sacrifice, the recitation, and likewise the accent,
where will the thunderbolt of speech not fall upon him, like [the bolt] of Śakra’s enemy?
(106) I shall now state for you, from the very beginning, the defining characteristics of those *yajus* formulas.
Having understood this, the wise man should apply it everywhere:
first the single syllable and so forth in sequence, then the *mā*, the *pramā*, and likewise the *pratimā*;
then the row of syllables with the vowel *ī*, and also the *gāyatrī* and *uṣṇih*. 107–108.
Anuṣṭubh, Bṛhatī, Paṅkti, Virāṭ, Triṣṭubh, as well as Jagatī, Atijagatī, Śakvarī, and likewise Atiśakvarī; Aṣṭi, Atyaṣṭi, Dhṛti, Atidhṛti, and likewise Kṛti. (109)
Prakṛti, ākṛti, vikṛti, saṃkṛti, atikṛti,
and utkṛti— these six are mentioned beyond the [standard] enumeration;
from this point upward, one should apply these as *aticchandas* among the *yajus* formulas.
I shall describe the Vedic meters, consisting of Ṛks and Sāmans; one should fill the verse with barley-grains.
It consists of four feet, each foot being composed of Ṛc verses, and it always exists as "Bhavat Preta" [in the ritual].
It may consist of one, two, three, or four feet, such as the Paṅkti and other meters, according to their respective parts. 112

All [the meters] increase by four; there are one hundred and four [syllables]. A *nimṛd* is deficient by one, and a *bhurik* is excessive by one. A *virāj* is deficient by five, and a *svarāj* is excessive by five. 113.

The *virāj* consists of two feet; it does not exist with fewer than five syllables per foot. When there are nine syllables per foot, it is proclaimed as *śakvarī*; when there are six and nine syllables, it is called *atijagatī*. Likewise, *vārāhī* would be situated [with] six and nine syllables. If there are three feet with fewer syllables in the middle foot, it is indeed *gāyatrī*.
That [meter] is to be known as *pipīlikā*, and it is characterized by an excess in the middle *yava*.
This same [structure] applies to all; now I shall describe each one individually.
Thus, the *gāyatrī* consists of three feet of six syllables each, and likewise [the *anuṣṭubh*] consists of three feet of eight syllables each.
That which consists of six, seven, and eleven syllables [per quarter] is to be known as Uṣṇiggarbhā;
likewise, that which consists of eight and twelve syllables per quarter is Virāṇrāmadvipādi.
Furthermore, there is a meter with three quarters of ten syllables each, and likewise with three quarters of eleven syllables each.
But by means of the groups of eight and twelve, there should be a *jagatī* in the middle of the two groups of nine;
indeed,
that is to be known as the *virāṭ* form of the *gāyatrī* itself when its form is lost.
That same [Pādanivṛt] becomes Pādanivṛt when it consists of three feet of seven syllables each.

(119) When there is a group of six in the middle of the [first two feet], it becomes Atinidhanā. Vardhamānā is to be known as that which has three feet of six, seven, and five syllables respectively. (120)
By these very same [syllables] reversed, that *sāmnī* is proclaimed;
the *uṣṇih* is to be known as having seven syllables, but by adding one more, if there are twelve syllables, [it becomes the *bṛhatī*]. 121.
If there are two groups of eight syllables at the beginning, middle, and end,
with a *kakuṃ* (jagatī) first and a *pūrvā* (triṣṭubh) last, it is proclaimed as the *uṣṇih*;
however, that which consists of three groups of eight and one group of five is to be known as the *uṣṇigārbhā*.
The *uṣṇih* consists of three feet of eleven, twelve, and four syllables respectively;
however, when it has two feet of eleven syllables each, it is known there as the *kakub*, *dvāku*, or *śiras*. (123–124)
The third [foot] shall consist of six syllables; thus is the *uṣṇih* illustrated.

From eight syllables, however, there arises the *anuṣṭubh*, provided that one [foot] consists of eight syllables. If there should be two feet of twelve syllables each, it is likewise called *ādyamahī* at the beginning and at the end.
The *kakubh* is known as being before, after, or at the beginning; it should be understood as belonging to the *anuṣṭubh*.
When there are two [feet] of twelve syllables and one of eight, that is the *kṛti-anuṣṭubh*. When there is one *gāyatrī* and three [feet] of eight syllables, that is the *ānuṣṭubha*. 126–127.
In some cases, it is proclaimed that the *anuṣṭubh* is at the beginning and the *pragātha* follows;
if there are eight *tvaṣṭaka* verses, the *bṛhatī* should consist of nine syllables.
If the *pathyā* is at the front and the *pariṣṭā* is at the end, it is as before, consisting of twelve syllables.
That which was previously taught as Tryaṅkusāriṇī is known as Pūrvā; it consists of three feet of twelve syllables each and two feet of ten syllables each, and is remembered as Viṣṭārā. 129–130.
The eightfold [set], the fourfold, and the great eightfold in the world;
the three eights, the two twelves, and the one preceded by seven hundred; the ninefold, the eightfold, the tenfold, and likewise the eightfold. (131)

The *bṛhatī* is declared by the exponents of the Vedas to have uneven feet; it consists of 132 [mātrās]. A *pragātha* beginning with a *bṛhatī* is called *nastṛta*; however, those *pragāthas* that begin with two *kakubh*s are known as *kākubha*.
If there are two Bṛhatīs preceded by a Mahā, both being ten-syllabled, they are known as [the Bṛhatī]; likewise, five Pañcas and five Aras are also [Bṛhatīs].
Furthermore, a Virāj is described as consisting of four ten-syllabled [Padas], and it is exactly like that.
Where there are two sets of twelve syllables in each of the feet of eight syllables,
arranged either in pairs or by twos, with *ya* at the beginning and likewise *ta* in the middle, and *sa* and *ta* at the end—
this is the *saṃstāra* and likewise the *prastāra*. 135.
The *paṅkti* meter preceded by *tāra* (the long syllable) is known to be of six kinds:
it consists of four, five, or two [syllables], with the preceding syllable being the *paṅkti*; likewise, it may consist of four, six, three, or five syllables. (136–137)
The sequence of feet should be known as follows: five pentads of syllables, then four pentads and a hexad; likewise, that which begins with "mahā" [is] the same.
Then there is an octad, a heptad, a hexad, a decad, and a nonad.

A *daśapakti* preceded by *mahā-* has been declared by those who know the meters [to be a specific variety]. (139) That which consists of five feet of eight syllables each is to be known as a *paṅkti*;
however, a *paṅkti* consisting of six feet of eight syllables each is to be known as a *viṣṭārapaṅkti*. (140)
The *virāṭ* form consists of ten, eight, five, three, eight syllables, four, and finally twelve syllables;
it should be known as the pure *triṣṭubh*, consisting of eleven syllables. 141.
When there are two groups of ten and one group of twelve, it is called *sābhisāriṇī*.
When there are two groups of nine and one group of ten, it is born from the *virāṭ* position;
provided that after three octosyllabic feet, there are two dodecasyllabic feet. (142–143)
That [meter] is to be known as the pure *jagatī* consisting of twelve syllables.

If there are *iṣṭakās* at the beginning, middle, and end of both the *jagatī* and the *triṣṭubh*, one should know it as *jyotiṣmatī*; if they are at the end, it is *adhipūrvikā*. All these indeed consist of four feet, having been fashioned from the *ṛk*. 144.
The others increase by four syllables; beyond that is the *ati-chandas*.

There are exactly seven meters beginning with the *gāyatrī*, and they are produced by increasing the number of syllables in sequence, each subsequent meter having four more syllables than the preceding one. 145–146.
The Yajus formulas consist of fifteen Pādas, beginning with one and increasing by one in each subsequent formula;
likewise, there are exactly seven Daiva formulas, which also begin with one and increase by one in sequence. (147)
In the same way, Matsya should understand that there is a gradual decrease of the Yajus for the Asuras;
likewise, through the sequence of the elements (dhātu), one should know that the Sāmans increase by four, and the Ṛks increase by three starting from twelve and eighteen respectively. 148–149.
Those beginning with twenty-four [syllables] are composed by the Ṛṣis; likewise, the Brāhma consists of thirty-six syllables and is composed by six [Ṛṣis].

Agni, Soma, Savitṛ, Bṛhaspati, Mitra-Varuṇa, Indra, and the Viśvedevas—these are the deities of the seven [chandas]. For men, the Ādityas [are the deities]; and for those consisting of a single word, Brahmā and Virāṭ are always [the deities]. 150–151.

Vāyu is the *vicchanda* (dispersed meter); indeed, the other meters are the *dhātṛ* (creator). White, with its limbs and marks, black, red, blue, and golden—these are the seven colors of purity. The *pṛśni*, the *vabhru*, and the *nakula* are the *virāj*;
the *ekapadā* and the *śāvanya* are others. This is the progeny of the meters, the seerhood (*ārṣa*). The god is concealed; death is in fear.

Those who, by means of those [mantras], mentally assume the nature of the mantra— the third [stage] called the "obstructing of the destination of premature death"— they are protected according to the rule as they have been described; and the Brahmin, having properly performed the prescribed rites and joined with the appropriate logical arguments and explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), [attains the goal].

I shall explain the accomplishment of the Pāpaṇya [mantras] according to the sequence of the essence of words and sentences, as they are said to be of two kinds: (155) some are for the consecration of substances, while many are for the exhaustion of the name of the deity; such as "viṣṇurmanasi" and "agnirbhava," which are to be understood in their proper order. These, however, are of three types: those performed indirectly (*parokṣa*), those performed directly (*pratyakṣa*), and those pertaining to the self (*ātmika*), which are few. (156)
The verb is joined with the first person [of the optative] and all the case-endings of the noun:
"Sūrya is the self for all to see," "he strives toward Sūrya," "milk by means of Sūrya," "the Sūryās," "those rays of yours, O Sūrya," and "the beloved of Sūrya. (157–158)

Those [verbs] formed with the remote [person], which are joined with the second person (*madhyama-puruṣa*) by means of the pronoun *tvam*, are called *adramāḥ* (those referring to the non-present); for example, "you have conquered" (*tvam ayodhayaḥ*). Similarly, those [verbs] formed with the highest person (*uttama-puruṣa*) by means of the pronoun *aham* are called *ādhyātmikāḥ*; for example, "I have conquered" (*aham ayodham*), or "I have known the waters" (*aham apas tattvā vidvān*). Furthermore, these four types are to be understood as occurring through various permutations (*paryāya*) in discourse, and they are to be known according to the completion of the sentence (*vākya-samāpti*). 159.

*rājñāsī* is a synonym for *paryāya*; *asītimravād* is [the end of] the *ugra*; the completion of your speech is *svachandochanda*. *Chandas* is of two kinds: those with one, two, three, four, five, or six feet; they have two pauses or three pauses; those that are equal are *sacchandāḥ*, while those with unequal syllables are *vicchandāḥ*.

These are well-known as fivefold: the *saumya*, the *amūḍha*, the *caturhotṛ*, the *cātugā*, and the *svaptyavadāna*. (161) The *saumya* mantras begin with "O Agni, come hither" (*agna āyāhi*); the *mūḍha* are the *caturhotṛ* mantras; the *cātugā* are those beginning with "the four satisfactions" (*catustṛptavat*); and the *svaptyavadāna* are the *ghora-aghoratara* mantras beginning with "O thou who art most terrible" (*ghoratama*). These latter are the *ābhicārika* (malevolent) rites. (162)
Thus, there are eighty-one of these; they are to be designated as follows: concerning Brahman, concerning sacrifice, concerning the deities, and concerning the self; then the eighties:

the curse, the malevolent rite, the ritual injunction, the pacification, the desire to know, 163 the etymological derivation, the division, the explanation of the *pṛśni* verses, the command, the reviling, the ascending after death, and the private recitation.

Praise, censure, two types of praise, speaking ill of others, purity, conceptualization, volition, enumeration, persistence, calling by name, begging, conversation, procreation, accumulation, retinue, shame, (164) addressing,
doubt, lamentation, and command.
Commanding, following after, looking [longingly], longing, conversation, lamentation;
165 prohibition, instruction, self-praise, salutation, being feverish, joy, astonishment, dismissal;
166 overwhelming, consultation, inquiry, refusal, recounting one’s own deeds, and contradiction.
The *amaharava*, the *ahanasya*, the *bhadra*, the *acārtha*, the *pasamṛddhi*, and the *alaṃkāra*—these six;

then the *upamārthaya*, the *kaṇḍīpaka*, the *yamaka*, the *samarthau*, the three genders in the tenth [chapter], the threefold time, and the fourfold word—these thirty-two [topics] comprise eighty-one [verses]. 167–168.

It is appropriate to define [the following]: the topic (*adhikaraṇa*), the application (*yoga*), the meaning of the term (*padārtha*), the meaning of the reason (*hetvartha*), the enunciation (*uddeśa*), the specification (*nirdeśa*), the instruction (*upadeśa*), the refutation (*apadeśa*), the location (*pradeśa*), the extension (*atideśa*), the conclusion (*upavarga*), the sentence-meaning (*vākyaśeṣa*), the inclusion (*arthāpatti*), the topical connection (*prasaṅga*), the one-sided view (*ekānta*), the non-one-sided view (*anekānta*), the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), the final determination (*nirṇaya*), the contrary position (*viparyaya*), the observation of similarity (*tattvāvekṣaṇa*), the observation of dissimilarity (*atattvāvekṣaṇa*), the prescription (*vidhāna*), and doubt (*saṃśaya*). 169–170.
Exegesis, approval, one’s own definition, etymological derivation, illustration, injunction, option, and conjunction—these indeed constitute my [method].
Of these, two are the means for the establishment of the meaning: the etymological and that which is sung by the seers (the *Ṛgveda*). 171.

"‘Puru’, ‘Gauḥ’, and ‘Iti’—all this is taught as tenfold: the innate (*autpattika*), the secondary (*gauṇa*), the occasional (*naimittika*), the devoted (*bhakta*), the conversational (*saṃvāda*), the indicative (*kānnaka*), the restrictive (*taśopavāra*), the connected (*sasambandha*), the sacrificial (*kravya*), and the technical (*yogika*). Among these, six means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) are to be known for their establishment: perception (*pratyakṣa*), inference (*anumāna*), tradition (*smṛti*), comparison (*upamāna*), postulation (*arthāpatti*), and analogy (*upamā*); as well as the supernormal tradition (*atismṛti*). [172–173]

Presumption (pratibhāṣa), probability (saṃbhava), existence (bhāva), postulation (arthāpatti), comparison (upamāna), gesture (iṣṭā)—these eight, as well as ten others, and four others, or these four, are declared by the Veda; tradition (smṛti), perception (pratyakṣa), inference (aitihya), and the fourfold means of knowledge for the sake of the object—this is the Vedic revelation, and the nature of Manu is the fourth. 174.
I shall explain all these means for the knowledge of speech; now I will provide examples for them:

the radiant Vedic knowledge is both direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and indirect inference (*parokṣa*), consisting of two types—the mere mark (*liṅgamātra*) and the knowledge of Brahman born of the seers (*ṛṣitamāna*). Even by a single word, that which is proclaimed as having many deities—Brahmā among the gods and the host of seers—is made manifest.

I ask you concerning that which is written, endowed with the divisions of the *yantras*, the throat of the sons of the sages being restrained like a *niyāta*. One should cause the *naigama* to revolve, beginning with those mixed [texts], the knowledge of the past, future, and present.
May they attain their own intention in the east.
175. Oṃ! The *nirbrahmasāvitrī*, the *vyāhṛtis*, and the *adhvaryu-yajña* have been declared in the *Puruṣasūkta*; the *haṃsa* is the celestial (*adhidaivya*).

[The commentary] subsequently explains the internal (*adhyātma*) meanings of the hymns to Rudra, the blessings for the sacrificer, the state of lying down, the granting of wealth, the protection from drought, and the [protection against] him who hates us, as well as curses and malevolent spells. Regarding the divine [nature], [the text says] "May that favor be ours," "May there be well-being for us," and "We do not know him," and so forth. When there is a double etymology (*nirvacana*), there is likewise a division [of the text]. In the case of a question such as "I ask this," if there is no explanation from the questioner, [it refers to] this command; "this is a cry," "this is a reproach," "the mother," "the woman who is being measured," and "the wife of those ascending after. Her own...

The *rohāva-pāvamānī* verses; the praise of Vedic study (*svādhyāya*); the non-censure of the verse beginning with *natā arva*; the praise [of the verse] "Surely he exists" (*nūnam asti*); the lamentation "There is no one now"; the binding of the *vrata* with the verse beginning "O Agni, come hither" (*agna āyāhi*); the purification by means of fire; the two options regarding the *drupadā* verses; the true resolve for blessings (*satyāśīḥ-saṃkalpa*); the enumeration; the connection [of the verse] "This very one they measure" (*imām eṣante yam*); the ritual action; the invocation of Indra with the verse "O Agni, come hither" (*agna āyāhi*); the invitation; the request; birth through progeny and so forth; the dialogue beginning with "With what [way]? (*kayāthvābhīyam*); the hymn; the *praśava-stava-prayāja* and so forth; the combination with the verse "King Soma" (*somam rājānam*); and the verse "Making a banner" (*ketum kṛṇvanti*). 176.

*Vādaḥ* (debate) is *vrīḍe* (shame); *yatkiṃcedam* (whatever this is) is *kāmayaṃtu* (let them desire); *vā* (or) is *āmantraṇam* (an address); *agneḥ* (of Agni) is *sahasrākṣaḥ* (the thousand-eyed one); *saṃśayaḥ* (doubt) is *kiṃsvit* (what indeed); *tvam* (you) is *ava* (down); *khiḥ* (kh) is *pralāpaḥ* (incoherent speech); *ca* (and) is *ekaḥ* (one); *adya* (today) is *pravalikā* (a small branch); *viyogam* (separation) is *imam* (this); *nraḥ* (man) is *uttame pāde* (in the last foot); *niyogaḥ* (application) is *idam* (this);

*bravīti* (he speaks) and so forth is *ādikam* (beginning with); *kadācana* (at any time) is *upadhāvanam* (running toward); *kasya* (of whom) is *styas* (is not); *aspṛhā* (desirelessness) is *tvā* (you); *bhūḥ* (earth) is *eti* (goes); *svadevaḥ* (own god) is *vā* (or); *vilāpam* (lamentation) is *nadasya* (of the river) and so forth; *iti* (thus) is *ādi-saṃjñāyaḥ* (the beginning of the technical designations).

Beholding those two, as well as the instructions and communications regarding the Ādityas, the embryo of the limbs, and the self-praise of the Śiro-medhas; "I have made obeisance"—thus he utters it with power. I do not know the fever that afflicts the one who is to be known; I take hold of the joy of both. "The slayer of the wind, the source of wonder—who indeed is the one who releases? Thus, O gods, may there be a path for us; let there be mutual agreement between me and you.

This is to be understood: "O Indra, bring [the prize]! Such is the command, and likewise the refusal: "He has struck. That which is to be known by the gods is the proclamation of one's own deed; what then shall be our protection against injury?

The joy of song, the removal of fear, great [fortune], not a small day, auspiciousness, the blessed one, of form, for the god, life-span, comparison, indeed, from the highest seat, he who abandons the body, he would act thus, devoid of [sin], Soma the god, not the sun—thus [are] the common [terms]. Indeed, Parjanya is not surpassed; the Brahmins move without wounds, for the sake of the meaning of the various forms of the complete ritual, they polish the single form upon the altar-ground. 177 This is the lamp-like *yamaka* (rhyme), the great *rūpaka* (metaphor) with many meanings, the self-practiced, and the variegated victory over the feminine, masculine, and neuter genders.

However, time consists of the past (*bhūta*), the present (*bhavat*), and the future (*bhaviṣyat*). In the phrase "sacrifice with sacrifice" (*yajñena yajñam*), there is the past; in "the cow is led away" (*gāṃ nīyate*), there is the present; and in "come, O slaughterer" (*āghātāgaccha*), there are such [forms]. These are nouns (*nāman*), verbs (*ākhyāta*), and particles (*nipāta*). A word (*pada*) is that which has been uttered by Yama; it is of two kinds: simple (*kevala*) and compound (*samasta*). A word is the designator (*abhidhāyaka*) of a substance (*dravya*), being suitable for its function through the eight case-endings (*vibhakti*), distinct in gender (*liṅga*) and number (*vacana*). Among these, we understand the name (*nāman*) as it truly is, from its beginning to its end, since it is perceived from whatever [source] it arises.
The feminine form arises from the verbal root through the suffix *kvi*, while the masculine form is derived from the gender; the neuter is distinct from both in terms of time.
However, by their very nature, those [particles] joined with meaning produce a specific sense for the two [genders].

The prefixes (*pra* etc. and the particles (*ca* etc. are indeed indeclinables; they serve four purposes: conjunction and so forth, filling out the meter, indicating a specific meaning, and negation. This is the etymological explanation (*nirukta*) regarding their purpose as already stated.
The meaning is established by the introduction of phonemes (*vyañjana*); it is like the sun illuminating a jewel, and thus it is to be restrained.

(181) One [syllable] is separated; the "throwing of the dog" (*śunaśchepa*) is explained by its cause, therefore [it refers to] the waters. Indeed, the introduction of phonemes is like Indra giving away Tārā from her debt; thus, indeed, is that which is to be known. (182)

Having struck down the Daitya Dhaivatu, the one whose conduct is like that of a bull among the excellent ones (Ativarokṣavṛtti) [is] beyond perception; for the manifestation of Māyā is indirect, whereas the Vācaḥ (Speech) is manifest. Thus, the Naigama [portion] consisting of ten divisions has been understood; it is designated as "Naigama" because its subject matter consists of word-classes (*padajāti*). By this [treatise], the first [section] is established through accent (*svarāt*), refinement (*saṃskāreṇa*), honor (*mānya*), the peak (*kakuḍatī*), multiplication (*guṇana*), and delusion (*moha*)—cease [your inquiry] according to this sequential division.

By "dispersion" (vikṣepaṇa), [the rule] "dyāvā naḥ pṛthivī... applies; by "non-dispersion" (avyavahara), [the rule] "vāyuḥ pūṣo me... applies. The remainder regarding the directions has been stated. When there is elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-lopa*), it occurs at the end of the elision; indeed, when there is elision of the final vowel (*anta-lopa*), it is reached [by that rule]. The section on the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-adhikāra*) begins with the word *rāja*. When a vowel is elided, as in *yāmi*, and when there is elision of two consonants (*udvivarṇa-lopa*), and in the reversal of *jyotis* and so forth.

In the *Viparyaya* (Reversal) variety of *Stokādimant*, there is the eating of men by a heavy woman; thus, from one [verse], there are two, and from two, one, with the reversal of case-endings (*vibhakti-viparyaya*) as in the *Hṛt-kha-śloka*. 185.
The example for the fifth [variety] is concluded.
Thus ends the Laugākṣi Śikṣā.
